title: Normal projective preparation and locality for valuation-curve modifications
statement:
Let $K$ be a separably closed [def-kun-separably-closed] field [def-weil-field] and $V\subset K$ a valuation ring with fraction field $K$: for every $a\in K^	imes$, either $a$ or $a^{-1}$ lies in $V$. Assume that the prime ideals of $V$ form a finite chain, and put $T=\operatorname{Spec}V$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum], with generic point $\eta=\operatorname{Spec}K$. Let $X$ be a $T$-curve with smooth generic fibre. Its normalization $X^
u	o X$ is a finite $\eta$-modification, $X^
u$ is normal, and $X^
u$ is a $T$-curve with geometrically reduced fibres. More generally, if $g:Y	o X$ is an $\eta$-modification whose source $Y$ is normal, then $g$ factors uniquely through $X^
u$. If $X$ is normal and affine, it is an open subscheme of a normal projective $T$-curve $\overline X$ with geometrically reduced fibres. Here projective means admitting a closed immersion into some $\mathbf P^n_T$ [def-pc-projective-morphism].
For an $\eta$-modification $f:Y	o X$ between normal $T$-curves with smooth generic fibres, the modification locus (the smallest closed subset off which $f$ is an isomorphism) is a finite set, quasi-finite over $T$ (finite type with finite fibres). Given a closed point $x$ of that locus, with image $s\in T$, the diagram can be studied after replacing $V$ by $V_s$ and shrinking $X$ about $x$ so that $X$ is connected affine and $x$ is its only closed modification point. The restricted modification extends to $\overline X$ by the identity off $X$, giving a normal proper $T$-curve $\overline Y$ with geometrically reduced fibres. Normal intermediate $\eta$-modification diagrams of this extended diagram restrict to the original open. The localization $\operatorname{Spec}V_s	o T$ is an open immersion, so the localized neighbourhood is already an open subscheme $U$ of the original $X$. The precise gluing assertion is the following. Let $W\subset X$ be closed with $x\in W\subset U$, and require $X\setminus W$ and $U\setminus W$ to be quasi-compact. For a restricted intermediate diagram $Y_U\xrightarrow{h_U}Z_U\xrightarrow{k_U}U$ of normal $\eta$-modifications, suppose that $h_U$ is an isomorphism over $U\setminus W$. Then it glues with the identity of $Y_{X\setminus W}$, using this specified isomorphism on the overlap, to normal $\eta$-modifications $Y\xrightarrow h Z\xrightarrow k X$ with $kh=f$. The diagram near $f^{-1}(x)$ is unchanged and $h$ is an isomorphism over $X\setminus W$. In particular this conclusion has support over generalizations of $x$ whenever $W$ is contained in that set. Identity on the isomorphism locus of $f$ alone is not a substitute for the overlap condition. For multipointed curves assume also that the generic marking is etale; the normalization, compactification, restriction and compatible gluing constructions carry the schematic closures of the generic markings on their intermediate curves. A $T$-curve means a flat [def-weil-flat-morphism] finitely presented [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation] $T$-scheme of pure relative dimension one [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. A geometric fibre is the base change of a fibre to an algebraic closure of its residue field [def-weil-geometric-fibre]; geometrically reduced means all such fibres have no nonzero nilpotents. An $\eta$-modification is a proper morphism [def-weil-proper-morphism] which is an isomorphism over the generic fibre and over schematically dense open subschemes; schematic density means injectivity of $\mathcal O_Z	o j_*\mathcal O_U$ for the open inclusion. A scheme is normal if every local ring is an integrally closed domain [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]. Its normalization means the scheme obtained by taking the integral closure of its structure sheaf in the product of the function fields of its irreducible components; for an integral scheme this is [def-sc-normalization]. A multipointed curve $(X,D)$ over a scheme $T$ means flat [def-weil-flat-morphism] finitely presented [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation] morphisms $X	o T$, $D	o T$ of pure relative dimensions $1$, $0$ and a closed immersion $D\hookrightarrow X$ [def-weil-closed-immersion]; $D$ may be empty and $X$ need not be separated or proper over $T$. It is semistable if every singular point of every geometric fibre has completed local ring $\Omega[[u,v]]/(uv)$ over its algebraically closed residue field, $D	o T$ is etale [def-weil-etale-morphism], and $D$ lies in the relative smooth locus [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]. For integral $T$ with generic point $\eta$, an $\eta$-modification of multipointed curves is a compatible pair $f_X:X'	o X$, $f_D:D'	o D$ of proper morphisms [def-weil-proper-morphism], each an isomorphism over a schematically dense open and on its generic fibre. A semistable such modification is stable if in each geometric fibre there is no irreducible component isomorphic to $\mathbf P^1$ that is contracted by $f_X$ and meets the union of the marking and the singular points of $X'$ in at most two points. Geometric fibres are [def-weil-geometric-fibre]; dimension is topological Krull dimension [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]; the local completion is at the maximal ideal [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion], and $\Omega[[u,v]]$ denotes the two-variable formal power series ring [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series]. Here an open immersion $j:U\hookrightarrow Z$ is schematically dense when $\mathcal O_Z	o j_*\mathcal O_U$ is injective.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1(i),(ii), printed p. 30; the normalization universal-property factorization for a normal modification source is used in Proposition 4.3.1, pp. 27--28; Lemma 4.2.1 and the following locality observation, printed p. 26; local reduction in the proof of Proposition 4.4.6, printed p. 32; primary PDF read online; local archival copy WANTED (report.md).

proof.text: The ring $V$ and its localizations are normal domains. Indeed, if an integral element $b$ of the fraction field is outside a valuation ring, $b^{-1}$ lies in its maximal ideal; dividing a monic equation by its leading power gives $1$ in that maximal ideal. The base is affine, integral and qcqs. The generic point is a principal open: choose an element of the smallest nonzero prime, or use $T=\eta$ if $V$ is a field. Flatness gives $A\hookrightarrow A_K$ for every affine ring of $X$, by torsion-freeness and the localization base-change formula. Hence $X_\eta$ is schematically dense, $X$ is reduced because $X_\eta$ is reduced, and every nonempty affine open meets $X_\eta$. The empty curve satisfies the normalization assertions vacuously.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1 and the local reductions preceding Lemma 4.4.2 and Proposition 4.4.6; agent expansion

proof.text: For nonempty $X$, apply the reduced-fibre modification theorem to $X\to T$. It is dominant by the preceding injectivity, finitely presented by hypothesis, and has geometrically reduced generic fibre by smoothness. Obtain $r:T'\to T$ and a finite generic-fibre isomorphism $Q'\to X\times_TT'$ with $Q'/T'$ flat finitely presented and with reduced geometric fibres. The generic field of $T'$ is a finite separable extension of $K$, hence is $K$. The proper valuative criterion extends this generic section to $\sigma:T\to T'$. Pulling back along $\sigma$ gives a finite map $q:Q\to X$, an isomorphism over $X_\eta$, with $Q/T$ flat finitely presented and geometrically reduced fibres. Flatness is preserved by tensor base change, finite presentation and geometric reducedness by the cited base-change statements.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1 and the local reductions preceding Lemma 4.4.2 and Proposition 4.4.6; agent expansion

proof.text: Apply generic normality of geometrically reduced families to $Q/T$. It is reduced and every finite $\eta$-modification of $Q$ is an isomorphism. Its generic fibre is normal by smoothness. The same theorem applies separately to every affine open of $Q$: restriction preserves flatness and reduced geometric fibres; affine source and base give qcqs, so the locally finitely presented restriction is finitely presented. On an affine open $\operatorname{Spec}B\subset Q$, flatness gives $B\hookrightarrow B_K$. The smooth affine generic fibre is Noetherian, so has finitely many irreducible components; normal local rings are domains, so two such components cannot meet (at a common point their distinct minimal primes would give distinct minimal primes of the local ring). Thus these finitely many components are disjoint open-and-closed integral normal schemes and $B_K$ is a finite product of normal domains.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1 and the local reductions preceding Lemma 4.4.2 and Proposition 4.4.6; agent expansion

proof.text: Each component idempotent $e\in B_K$ satisfies $e^2-e=0$. Consequently $B[e]$ is finite over $B$ and is a subalgebra of $B_K$. It agrees with $B$ after inverting one nonzero element $a\in V$. Multiplication by $a$ is injective in both rings, so $D(a)$ is schematically dense on both spectra. The finite map is proper and is a finite $\eta$-modification. The preceding $\eta$-normality makes it an isomorphism. Hence all these idempotents lie in $B$, which therefore decomposes as a finite product $\prod_iB_i$ of domains with $(B_i)_K$ normal domains.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1 and the local reductions preceding Lemma 4.4.2 and Proposition 4.4.6; agent expansion

proof.text: If $b\in\operatorname{Frac}(B_i)$ is integral over $B_i$, it is integral over the normal domain $(B_i)_K$, whose fraction field is the same, and therefore belongs to $(B_i)_K$. Write $b=c/a$ with $c\in B_i$ and $a\in V\setminus0$. The finite algebra $B_i[b]$ is a subring of this fraction field and equals $B_i$ over $D(a)$; as above it defines a finite $\eta$-modification of the open-and-closed component. Extend it by the identity on the other components to apply the $\eta$-normality of $\operatorname{Spec}B$. Thus $b\in B_i$. Integral closure commutes with localization, so every local ring of $B$ is an integrally closed domain. This proves $Q$ normal. The argument of these two steps uses only normality of $Q_\eta$, not smoothness.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1 and the local reductions preceding Lemma 4.4.2 and Proposition 4.4.6; agent expansion

proof.text: On an affine open $\operatorname{Spec}A\subset X$ the finite preimage is $\operatorname{Spec}B$. The generic isomorphism identifies both algebras inside the product of the function fields of the generic components. The algebra $B$ is integral over $A$, hence contained in its integral closure. Conversely any element of that product integral over $A$ is integral over $B$ and belongs to $B$, since the normal factors of $B$ are integrally closed. Thus $B$ is exactly the integral closure of $A$. The identifications agree on localizations, so $Q=X^\nu$ with the normalization convention in the statement. The map is finite proper, generically an isomorphism between schematically dense opens. Its source is flat finitely presented; its generic fibre has pure dimension one, so the dense-generic-fibre dimension theorem gives the same purity on all fibres. This proves the normalization clause, including geometrically reduced fibres.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1 and the local reductions preceding Lemma 4.4.2 and Proposition 4.4.6; agent expansion

proof.text:
For a normal modification source $Y$, there are finitely many components, by the horizontal curve-model statement with empty marking. They are disjoint open and closed: every local ring is a domain and a point cannot lie on two of finitely many components. Each component maps dominantly to the corresponding reduced component of $X$; the defining ideal of that reduced component pulls back to zero because it vanishes on the dense generic fibre and $Y$ is reduced. Apply the dominant normalization lifting theorem on each component. The componentwise normalizations form $X^
u$, so the lifts give $Y	o X^
u$. Uniqueness follows componentwise from the same theorem, or from schematic density and separatedness of the finite map $X^
u	o X$.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1 and the local reductions preceding Lemma 4.4.2 and Proposition 4.4.6; agent expansion

proof.text: Now let $X$ be normal affine. For empty $X$, use the empty closed subscheme of $\mathbf P^0_T$ as its compactification. Otherwise choose finitely many generators of its finite-type $V$-algebra to embed it as a closed subscheme of $\mathbf A^n_T$. Take its schematic closure $C'\subset\mathbf P^n_T$. The schematic-image theorem gives a schematically dense open immersion $X\hookrightarrow C'$. On each standard affine chart, the closure ring injects into the ring of sections on its intersection with $X$ and then into the generic-fibre sections. Hence it is $V$-torsion-free, and is flat over $V$. It is a finite-type $V$-algebra. Apply the finite-type module presentation theorem to this algebra as a cyclic module over a polynomial $V$-algebra: its kernel ideal is finitely generated, so the chart algebra is finitely presented over $V$. Thus $C'/T$ is flat finitely presented and projective.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1 and the local reductions preceding Lemma 4.4.2 and Proposition 4.4.6; agent expansion

proof.text: The generic closure $C'_\eta$ is reduced and has the same generic function fields as $X_\eta$. After any field extension each affine chart ring injects into the product of the corresponding generic function fields after scalar extension; these are reduced because they are localizations of the geometrically reduced $X_\eta$. Scalar extension preserves the injection. Thus $C'_\eta$ is geometrically reduced and pure one-dimensional. The dense-generic-fibre dimension theorem makes $C'$ a $T$-curve. Its generic fibre need not be normal at the boundary: this is why one must normalize the generic closure before invoking the normality argument above.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1 and the local reductions preceding Lemma 4.4.2 and Proposition 4.4.6; agent expansion

proof.text: Let $N_\eta\to C'_\eta$ be the normalization of the projective generic curve. It is finite, normal and projective by projective-curve normalization; it is an isomorphism on the normal open $X_\eta$. The same injection into the scalar-extended generic function fields shows that $N_\eta$ is geometrically reduced. On the quasi-compact open $O=X\cup C'_\eta\subset C'$ glue $X$ and $N_\eta$ along their identified opens $X_\eta$. Scheme gluing and morphism gluing produce a finite morphism $F\to O$: on the two target opens it is respectively the identity and the finite normalization. Finiteness is affine-local on the target, directly by gluing the finite algebra sheaves. It is separated and quasi-finite.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1 and the local reductions preceding Lemma 4.4.2 and Proposition 4.4.6; agent expansion

proof.text: The composite $F\to C'$ is separated quasi-finite and of finite type: $O\to C'$ is a quasi-compact open immersion and $F\to O$ is finite. Apply Zariski main to embed $F$ as a quasi-compact open in a finite $C'$-scheme $H$. Take the schematic closure $E$ of $F$ in $H$. Over $O$, the immersion $F\to H_O$ is proper: its graph is closed because $H_O/O$ is separated, and projection from $F\times_OH_O$ is the base change of the finite map $F\to O$. Hence it is a closed immersion. It follows that $E_O=F$, since the schematic closure restricts to the original closed subscheme there. The scheme $E$ is finite over $C'$ and has dense generic fibre $N_\eta$.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1 and the local reductions preceding Lemma 4.4.2 and Proposition 4.4.6; agent expansion

proof.text: The generic fibre is schematically dense in $E$: it is so in $F$ (locally this is $X$ or $N_\eta$), and $F$ is schematically dense in $E$. Therefore each affine ring of $E$ injects into its generic localization and is torsion-free over $V$. The torsion-free flatness theorem and the cyclic-polynomial-module argument of the closure step show that $E/T$ is flat and finitely presented. Its generic fibre is normal and geometrically reduced. Apply the reduced-fibre modification theorem to $E/T$, eliminate the separable base alteration with the proper valuative section as before, and obtain a finite $\eta$-modification $\bar X\to E$ with flat finitely presented source and geometrically reduced fibres. The idempotent and integral-element arguments above, now using normal $N_\eta$, show that $\bar X$ is normal. The dimension theorem makes it a $T$-curve.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1 and the local reductions preceding Lemma 4.4.2 and Proposition 4.4.6; agent expansion

proof.text: The map $\bar X\to C'$ is finite, and over the normal open $X$ it is an isomorphism. Indeed, componentwise this is a finite birational map onto a normal integral scheme, so the finite birational normal-target theorem applies. For projectivity, the finite map is projective in the projective-bundle convention. The projective scheme $C'$ over the affine base has an ample invertible sheaf; the projective-bundle-to-H-projective theorem therefore gives a closed immersion of $\bar X$ into a finite projective space over $C'$. Composing H-projective morphisms gives the required closed immersion into some $\mathbf P^m_T$. This uses no Noetherian hypothesis on $V$.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1 and the local reductions preceding Lemma 4.4.2 and Proposition 4.4.6; agent expansion

proof.text: For $f:Y\to X$ between normal curves, the horizontal curve-model theorem gives finitely many components of $X$. Apply the modification-locus theorem: its locus $L$ is quasi-finite over $T$. Since $T$ has finitely many points and every fibre of $L/T$ is finite, the set $|L|$ is finite. Give it its reduced closed structure. The locus has no point over $\eta$ because $f_\eta$ is an isomorphism.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1 and the local reductions preceding Lemma 4.4.2 and Proposition 4.4.6; agent expansion

proof.text: Let $x$ be closed in $L$ and let $s\in T$ be its image. It is closed in $X$ since $L$ is closed. The localization $\operatorname{Spec}V_s$ is an open of $T$: if there is a prime immediately above $s$, choose $a$ in it and outside $s$, giving $D(a)=\{t:t\text{ generalizes }s\}$; if $s$ is maximal use $D(1)$. Thus localization does not require spreading across an inverse limit. In the finite $T_0$-space $L$, the set of generalizations of $x$ is open (intersect all its finitely many open neighbourhoods). Realize it as $L\cap U_0$ for an open $U_0$ of $X$. Choose a connected affine neighbourhood $U$ of $x$ inside $U_0\times_T\operatorname{Spec}V_s$. Such a choice is possible because the finitely many normal components of $X$ are disjoint open and closed. Then $L_U$ has $x$ as its unique closed point.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1 and the local reductions preceding Lemma 4.4.2 and Proposition 4.4.6; agent expansion

proof.text: Over the localized base, $L_U$ is finite, not merely a finite topological set. To check this, the normal integral local scheme $\operatorname{Spec}V_s$ has separably closed function field $K$, so its local ring is strictly henselian by the etale-over-normal theorem. The separated quasi-finite affine scheme $L_U$ embeds openly in a finite scheme by Zariski main. A finite algebra over this henselian local ring splits as a product of local finite algebras. The closed point $x$ lies in one factor. An open containing the closed point of a local scheme is the entire factor. No point of another factor belongs to $L_U$, since the finite space $L_U$ has only one closed point and every point specializes to one. Therefore $L_U$ is that finite factor.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1 and the local reductions preceding Lemma 4.4.2 and Proposition 4.4.6; agent expansion

proof.text: Compactify the normal affine curve $U$ by the preceding construction over $V_s$, obtaining normal projective $\bar X$. The finite scheme $L_U$ over this base is closed in $\bar X$: its map has closed graph in $L_U\times_T\bar X$, since $\bar X/T$ is separated, and the projection to $\bar X$ is proper as a base change of $L_U/T$. Thus this map is proper and its image is closed. This justifies using $\bar X\setminus L_U$ as an open chart; finiteness of the set alone would not justify that step.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1 and the local reductions preceding Lemma 4.4.2 and Proposition 4.4.6; agent expansion

proof.text: Over $U\setminus L_U$ the map $f$ is the identity. Glue $Y_U$ to $\bar X\setminus L_U$ along this identification. Scheme gluing gives $\bar Y$, and morphism gluing gives $\bar f:\bar Y\to\bar X$. On the target cover $U,\bar X\setminus L_U$, the map is respectively the proper map $f_U$ and an identity. Thus it is proper by target locality; it is a generic-fibre isomorphism. The two charts are normal. The original normal $Y$ has geometrically reduced fibres by the normalization result proved above (its normalization is the identity), and the other chart inherits this property from $\bar X$. Flatness, local finite presentation and fibre purity are chart-local. The cover and its overlap are quasi-compact by the finite-algebra calculation in the next step, applied also in the finitely many affine charts of $\bar X$. Consequently the glued scheme is qcqs and finitely presented. It is a normal proper $T$-curve with geometrically reduced fibres, agreeing with $f$ near $f^{-1}(x)$.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1 and the local reductions preceding Lemma 4.4.2 and Proposition 4.4.6; agent expansion

proof.text:
For completeness, let $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ and $J$ define the finite subscheme $L_U$. Choose finite $V$-algebra generators $t_1,\ldots,t_n$ of $A$. Their images in the finite $V$-algebra $A/J$ satisfy monic equations $p_i$. Thus $I=(p_i(t_i))\subset J$ and $A/I$ is a finite $V$-module, generated by the monomials with each exponent below the degree of $p_i$. The finite scheme $H=V(I)$ has finitely many points, because $T$ is finite and its fibres are finite. The open $H\setminus L_U$ is therefore quasi-compact and is covered by finitely many $D(g_j)\cap H$ with $g_j\in J$. Now
$$U\setminus L_U=\bigcup_iD(p_i(t_i))\ \cup\ \bigcup_jD(g_j).$$
This finite basic-open cover proves the required quasi-compactness. The calculation works on every affine chart containing part of a finite closed subscheme.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1 and the local reductions preceding Lemma 4.4.2 and Proposition 4.4.6; agent expansion

proof.text: Any intermediate diagram of normal $\eta$-modifications of $\bar f$ restricts to $U$ by taking fibre products. Properness survives base change; the generic-fibre isomorphisms, flatness, finite presentation and geometric fibre properties restrict to opens. Schematic density restricts as injectivity of the restricted structure-sheaf map. Normality is local. Thus the restricted diagram is the asserted original local intermediate diagram.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1 and the local reductions preceding Lemma 4.4.2 and Proposition 4.4.6; agent expansion

proof.text: For the corrected global locality assertion, put $B=X\setminus W$. On $U\cap B=U\setminus W$, the given isomorphism $h_U$ identifies $(Z_U,k_U)$ with $(Y_U,f_U)$. Glue $Z_U$ and $Y_B$ using exactly this isomorphism, and glue their maps to $X$. Also glue $h_U$ and the identity of $Y_B$. The two-chart cocycle is just the chosen isomorphism and its inverse; both resulting compositions agree with $f$ on each chart, hence agree globally. This produces $Y\xrightarrow h Z\xrightarrow k X$ with $kh=f$. The explicit quasi-compact overlap assumptions give qcqs gluing and finite presentation. Its charts are normal flat finitely presented curves. Properness of $k$ is target-local on $U,B$, and properness of $h$ is target-local on the corresponding charts of $Z$. The generic fibres are identities between dense generic opens, so both maps are $\eta$-modifications. By construction $h$ is the identity over $B$, and restriction near $x$ recovers the prescribed local diagram.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1 and the local reductions preceding Lemma 4.4.2 and Proposition 4.4.6; agent expansion

proof.text: For the multipointed assertion, $D_\eta$ is finite etale over the separably closed field $K$, hence is a finite disjoint union of $K$-points. Each point extends uniquely to a section of the proper curve $\bar X$ by the proper separated valuative criterion. These sections are closed immersions since $\bar X/T$ is separated. Their schematic union is the closure of $D_\eta$: its local rings inject into products of the section rings and have no $V$-torsion. It is therefore flat by the valuation torsion-free criterion. It is proper as a closed subscheme of $\bar X$, of finite type, and has finite fibres (its support is the union of finitely many sections). Thus it is quasi-finite, and proper quasi-finite implies finite. On its affine coordinate ring apply the cyclic-polynomial-module finite-presentation argument used above. Its generic fibre is pure dimension zero, so the dense-generic-fibre dimension theorem gives pure relative dimension zero.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1 and the local reductions preceding Lemma 4.4.2 and Proposition 4.4.6; agent expansion

proof.text: Schematic generic closures are unique among flat closed subschemes: on an affine chart a flat quotient injects into its generic localization, so its ideal is the kernel of generic restriction. On every proper intermediate curve repeat the section-closure argument of the preceding step; it requires properness, not smoothness at the generic boundary. A map between these proper models sends the source marking into the target marking because the target ideal vanishes on the schematically dense generic marking. The induced marking map is proper: both markings are finite over $T$ and the target is separated, so use the closed graph and proper projection argument. It is generically an isomorphism. On models over the original smooth-generic open, the horizontal curve-model theorem gives the flat finitely presented marking and its proper modification maps. The uniqueness calculation identifies all these closures on the quasi-compact gluing overlaps. Gluing them supplies the multipointed diagrams. Empty marking stays empty.
